sketches.title: Emotion on the Lam
sketches.premise: A feeling has gone missing, and the Host is putting up a lost-and-found notice for it. Turn the dull clues into a dramatic notice that still makes the feeling identifiable, even while you give it a ridiculous new life.
sketches.criterion: The move must keep the named feeling identifiable as the feeling that is missing, without replacing it with a different feeling or merely commenting on the game.
sketches.move_shape: Write one lost-and-found notice under 90 characters, including a wild description, alleged last sighting, or reward; example: "MISSING: JEALOUSY—LAST SEEN COUNTING HER EX'S LIKES AT 2 A.M."
sketches.first_card: The feeling is mild embarrassment; the two nouns are a bus and a microphone.

sketches.title: Heartbreak Evidence Locker
sketches.premise: The Host found one emotion at a suspicious scene and needs a piece of evidence for the case. Submit a tiny evidence label that proves the feeling is there, while making the scene as tender, filthy, or absurd as you dare.
sketches.criterion: The move must preserve one concrete, readable sign of the dealt feeling at the scene; invented causes and details are welcome, but the sign cannot point to another feeling instead.
sketches.move_shape: Write an evidence tag under 90 characters; example: "ITEM 4: ONE UNOPENED TEXT, STILL SAVED AS 'DO NOT REPLY, YOU COWARD.'"
sketches.first_card: The feeling is homesickness; the two nouns are a suitcase and a spoon.

sketches.title: Mood Mugshot
sketches.premise: Every feeling has been booked, and the Host is taking its mugshot. Give the feeling a caption that keeps its identity clear but makes its crime, alibi, or bad attitude unforgettable.
sketches.criterion: The move must keep the dealt feeling recognizable as the person or force in the caption, not quietly swap it for a neighboring emotion.
sketches.move_shape: Write a mugshot caption under 90 characters; example: "ANGER, 34: WANTED FOR TURNING 'FINE' INTO A THREE-DAY WAR."
sketches.first_card: The feeling is relief; the two nouns are a dentist and a balloon.

sketches.title: The Feeling You Left Behind
sketches.premise: The Host is writing a note from a feeling that vanished after an ordinary moment. Make the note sound like that exact feeling speaking, with enough strange detail to suggest where it went.
sketches.criterion: The move must keep the dealt feeling as the note's speaker and emotional truth; the story may invent everything around it but may not contradict that feeling's presence or character.
sketches.move_shape: Write a farewell note under 90 characters; example: "I LEFT AFTER YOU SAID 'NO WORRIES' AND MEANT EVERY SINGLE WORRY."
sketches.first_card: The feeling is boredom; the two nouns are a fridge and a wedding.

sketches.title: Found Feeling for Sale
sketches.premise: The Host found a feeling in a junk shop and is listing it online. Write the listing so buyers can still tell what feeling it is, while the price, defects, and sales pitch go gloriously off the rails.
sketches.criterion: The move must retain the dealt feeling as the item being sold, with its emotional nature still readable; added claims are fair unless they erase or contradict that identity.
sketches.move_shape: Write a sale listing under 90 characters; example: "FOR SALE: REGRET, LIGHTLY USED, COMES WITH 400 PHOTOS YOU SHOULD'VE DELETED."
sketches.first_card: The feeling is pride; the two nouns are a trophy and a sandwich.

sketches.title: Wanted by the Heart
sketches.premise: The Host is making a wanted poster for a feeling that escaped into everyday life. Name its habits, hideout, or accomplices so the poster stays true while becoming a playful little manhunt.
sketches.criterion: The move must keep the named feeling as the wanted fugitive and preserve its recognizable emotional meaning; all surrounding motives and crimes may be invented.
sketches.move_shape: Write a wanted-poster line under 90 characters; example: "WANTED: LONELINESS, HIDING IN GROUP CHATS, ANSWERING EVERYONE WITH 'LOL.'"
sketches.first_card: The feeling is gratitude; the two nouns are a raincoat and a neighbor.
